anpr.warmup_note: First 5 detection frames and 3 OCR reads are DISCARDED. They include lazy model construction, Metal/CUDA kernel compilation and (for PaddleOCR) a possible one-time model download, none of which recur in a running deployment.

video.path: /Users/aarushsharma/Documents/SIH/archive/Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) _ Vehicle Number Plate Recognition (1).mp4

measured.method: cv2.VideoCapture.read() on 1280x720 H.264, 869 sequential frames, first 5 samples discarded

decode.why_it_matters: A central architecture pays this per camera per analysed frame before any inference happens; an edge architecture does not pay it centrally at all.

input_resolution.note: Detection cost is governed by yolo_imgsz (the letterboxed inference size), not by the source resolution — a 4K feed costs the same to infer at imgsz=640 but more to decode. Cost rises roughly with imgsz^2, so imgsz=1280 is ~4x the compute of imgsz=640.

measured_p50.method: YOLOv8s plate detector, device=mps, imgsz=640, 120 warm frames from real video

measured_p95.method: same run, nearest-rank p95 — this is the number used for capacity sizing, because sizing on a median under-provisions half the time

plates_detected_per_frame_mean.method: mean detections over the 120 timed frames of this specific clip

detection.plates_per_frame_caveat: This is what THIS clip contained, not a Delhi junction. The projection's `plates_per_frame` assumption is separate and deliberately not taken from here — one benchmark clip is not a traffic survey. Detection cost is one YOLO pass per frame either way; only OCR load depends on this number.

model_load_seconds.method: PlateDetector construction + first forward pass (worker cold-start cost)

process_cpu_seconds_per_frame.method: psutil user+system CPU time of this process across the timed detection loop, divided by frame count

cpu_cost.note: On Apple silicon part of this work is on the GPU via MPS, so CPU-seconds here understates total silicon used. It is still the right basis for sizing the CPU side of a worker.

measured_p50.method: PaddleOCR TextRecognition via alpr PlateReader.read(), 40 warm reads, includes crop+padding prep

measured_p95.method: same run, nearest-rank p95 — used for sizing

model_load_seconds.method: PaddleOCR model construction; includes a one-time download on a cold machine, which is why it is reported separately and excluded from per-crop timings

process_cpu_seconds_per_crop.method: psutil user+system CPU time across the timed OCR loop

ocr.note: PaddleOCR here runs on CPU, not MPS — so OCR throughput scales with cores, while detection scales with the accelerator. That is the single most important fact for sizing: the two stages are bottlenecked by different hardware.

pipeline_fps_ocr_every_1.caveat: Assumes exactly one plate read per OCR frame and no decode/IO overlap. The real alpr Pipeline also runs a tracker and a vote window, so treat this as an upper bound.

pipeline_fps_ocr_every_3.caveat: Assumes exactly one plate read per OCR frame and no decode/IO overlap. The real alpr Pipeline also runs a tracker and a vote window, so treat this as an upper bound.

detection_ms_per_frame.direction: we measured FASTER than the reference
detection_ms_per_frame.assessment: different but plausible (different chip / thermal state)

ocr_ms_per_crop.direction: we measured SLOWER than the reference

upstream_cross_check.note: Our measured numbers are the source of truth for every projection. The reference exists only to catch a broken measurement.

peak_rss_mb.method: resident set size of this process with the plate detector AND the PaddleOCR model loaded — the per-inference-worker RAM floor

ingest.work_per_event: camera lookup, row insert, MTMC plate/spatio-temporal association, blacklist check and checkpoint-pair speed/route-anomaly check
ingest.concurrency: single client, serial requests (no request-level parallelism)

events_per_second.method: 60 serial requests over 0.12s via fastapi.testclient (warmup excluded)

single.note: Serial throughput of ONE client. It is a per-event cost measurement, not the server's ceiling: a real deployment runs many workers concurrently, and the projection multiplies this out explicitly.

events_per_second.method: batch of 100 through POST /events/bulk-ingest, mean of 3 batches
batch of 500 through POST /events/bulk-ingest, mean of 3 batches
batch of 1000 through POST /events/bulk-ingest, mean of 3 batches

bulk.note: Per-event cost falls with batch size because the camera lookup and the commit amortise, but the per-event MTMC + alert queries do not — so the curve flattens rather than scaling linearly.

query.engine: sqlite (dev default) — Postgres numbers will differ, usually better for concurrent reads and worse for tiny single-row lookups

scaling.model: latency ≈ rows^k, fitted from exactly two points
scaling.two_point_caveat: Two points cannot distinguish a genuine power law from a constant plus a linear term. Treat k as a direction indicator, not a coefficient — and do not extrapolate it many orders of magnitude.

endpoints.name: summary
endpoints.verdict: LINEAR OR WORSE — will not survive city scale without a rollup table

query.row_count_caveat: Rows are synthetic and seeded by this benchmark into a temp database. The distribution (plates, cameras, 24h spread) is realistic in shape but not real traffic. Latency is only meaningful next to its row count.
query.known_limitation: heatmap, od-matrix and speed-defaulters aggregate in Python after loading rows, so their cost grows with rows returned, not with an index. That shows up directly in the two-scale comparison below and is the first thing to fix before a real city rollout.

bytes_per_event.method: temp benchmark sqlite file size / vehicle_events row count; includes indexes and the (tiny) other tables, so it slightly overstates the per-row cost

dev_db_cross_check.access: opened read-only (mode=ro); never written by the benchmark

bytes_per_event.method: real dev.db file size / row count

db_isolation.note: Measured against a throwaway sqlite database created for this run and deleted afterwards. dev.db was never opened for writing.

how_to_read_this.MEASURED: timed on the machine named in `hardware`, reproducible by re-running scripts/run_benchmarks.py
how_to_read_this.PROJECTED: arithmetic on MEASURED values plus the assumptions listed in each figure's `depends_on`
how_to_read_this.DERIVED: arithmetic on MEASURED values only, no external assumptions
how_to_read_this.rule: No number in this file was typed in by hand. If a suite did not run, its section holds an error, not a placeholder.

accelerator.note: Apple MPS (unified-memory GPU) is not comparable to a discrete datacentre GPU. Any GPU-count projection below is an assumption, not a measurement on this machine.

assumption_rationale.cameras: 200 = the real Delhi junctions currently in deployments/delhi/cameras.json. 500 and 2000 are modelled as growth scenarios.
assumption_rationale.fps_per_camera: ANPR does not need the full 30 fps. A vehicle crossing a junction approach stays plate-readable for roughly 1-2 seconds, so 6 analysed frames per second gives 6-12 independent chances to read the same plate — enough for the pipeline's multi-frame vote — at one fifth of the compute of 30 fps. Raise it for high-speed expressway cameras where the readable window is shorter.
assumption_rationale.ocr_every: OCR runs on every 3rd frame that contains a plate. The upstream repo measures ocr_every=3 as the sweet spot (23.5 vs 14.3 fps) because the vote window still collects several reads per vehicle pass.
assumption_rationale.plates_per_frame: Mean number of plates visible per analysed frame at a junction approach. Drives OCR load only — detection cost is one YOLO pass regardless.
assumption_rationale.vehicles_per_camera_per_hour: 1200 = 20 vehicles/minute past one camera. NOT measured by us; it sets the DB event rate. A quiet residential camera is far lower, a peak-hour arterial approach higher.
assumption_rationale.target_latency_s: End-to-end budget from photon to dashboard. 2 s is the operator requirement for a blacklist hit to be actionable. It constrains queue depth: a worker may not accumulate more than this much backlog.
assumption_rationale.utilisation_headroom: Size to 70% of measured capacity, never 100%. Headroom absorbs peak hour, thermal throttling, model reloads and node failure. Sizing at 100% guarantees the system falls behind exactly when it matters.
assumption_rationale.gpu_class: Which GPU the GPU-count projection assumes. We measured only this Mac, so this is a stated assumption.
assumption_rationale.gpu_speedup_vs_measured_device: How many times faster one such GPU is than the accelerator we measured, for this YOLOv8s workload. ASSUMPTION, NOT A MEASUREMENT — 3x for a T4 vs Apple MPS is a conservative published-throughput estimate. Anyone quoting a GPU count must quote this multiplier with it.
assumption_rationale.stream_bitrate_mbps: Per-camera H.264 bitrate for 1080p CCTV. 4 Mbps is typical for a traffic-grade encoder; 4K or low-compression feeds are several times higher.
assumption_rationale.event_wire_bytes: Size of one structured VehicleEvent JSON on the wire (~400 B observed for the ingest payload shape). Used for the edge-architecture uplink.
assumption_rationale.retention_days: How long events are kept before archival/rollup. 90 days.
assumption_rationale.replication_factor: 1.0 = single copy. Set to 3.0 for a replicated cluster.
assumption_rationale.hours_per_day: Hours per day cameras are analysed. 24 = always on. Night-only or peak-only operation scales cost down linearly.

required_ocr_throughput.formula: 1200 frames/s / ocr_every 3 x 1.5 plates per frame

cost_per_analysed_frame.formula: detection p95 24.88 ms + (1.5/3) x OCR p95 46.22 ms
cost_per_analysed_frame.caveat: Assumes detection and OCR share one worker process, as they do today.

workers_of_measured_class.unit: workers equivalent to the measured machine (Mac15,12)
workers_of_measured_class.caveat: This is the only worker-count figure grounded entirely in a measurement on real hardware. Everything GPU-related below applies an assumed multiplier to it.

inference.what_a_worker_is: One SERIAL pipeline slot: a process that decodes, detects and reads one frame at a time. The count is set by latency per frame, not by how much silicon a slot uses — see sizing_reconciliation, because N slots do NOT mean N physical machines.

sizing_reconciliation.binding_constraint_note: On the measured machine, RAM binds first. Each slot is a separate process that loads its own copy of the YOLO and PaddleOCR models — the measured RSS below. Sharing one model instance across threads would raise slots-per-host substantially and is the cheapest available optimisation, but we have not measured it, so it is not assumed here.

cpu_cores_consumed_per_slot.formula: 14.59 frames/s x 0.0321 measured core-seconds per frame (detection + its OCR share)

slots_per_host.unit: slots per host (8 cores, 17.18 GB RAM)
slots_per_host.caveat: ASSUMES PERFECT PARALLEL SCALING, WHICH WE DID NOT MEASURE. We ran one slot at a time. Real slots contend for one shared GPU/MPS queue and for memory bandwidth, so the true figure is lower. Measuring it needs a concurrency test that this suite does not yet run.

physical_hosts_of_measured_class.caveat: Upper-bound-optimistic for the same reason as slots_per_host.

sizing_reconciliation.why_this_block_exists: Without it, 'workers' and 'CPU cores' in this report look inconsistent. They are not: a slot is latency-bound and uses a fraction of a core.

gpus.assumption_warning: WE DID NOT MEASURE A DATACENTRE GPU. This count is the measured per-frame cost divided by an assumed 3.0x speedup for a NVIDIA T4 (16GB, inference-class). Treat the GPU count as a sizing estimate whose error bar is the multiplier's error bar. The worker count above is the honest, measured figure.

cpu_cores.formula: (1200 fps x 0.0086 core-s/frame + 600 crops/s x 0.0471 core-s/crop) / 0.7
cpu_cores.caveat: Derived from CPU time measured on Apple silicon, where some detection work runs on the GPU via MPS. On a CPU-only or CUDA server the split between cores and accelerator differs.

ram_gb.caveat: Excludes the database tier and OS overhead.

events_per_second.caveat: One event per vehicle per camera pass (the pipeline's vote window collapses many frames into one event), NOT one per frame.

measured_ingest_capacity.method: best measured throughput through the real ingestion endpoints on this machine (sqlite, single client)

ingest_headroom_ratio.caveat: Above 1.0 means one backend process on this laptop already keeps up. Below 1.0 means the write path needs sharding or Postgres + batching.

bytes_per_event.method: derived from an actual sqlite database file size / row count

storage.caveat: Structured events only. Storing plate crops or video clips is orders of magnitude larger and is a separate decision — a 50 KB JPEG per event would multiply this by ~100x.

measured_pipeline_ms.method: decode p50 0.9 + inference 48.0 + ingest p95 2.29 — measured stages, summed

max_queue_depth_frames.unit: frames of backlog a worker may hold
max_queue_depth_frames.caveat: Exceeding this means the plate arrives after the operator needs it, even though throughput looks fine. This is why sizing uses p95 and 70% headroom.

latency.note: This is the single-pass processing cost, not wall-clock photon-to-dashboard: it excludes camera encoder delay and network transit, which we cannot measure without real cameras.

central_architecture.description: Every camera streams video to a central GPU cluster, which decodes and runs ANPR.
central_architecture.extra_central_cost: The cluster also pays video DECODE for every analysed frame — measured separately in the anpr suite's decode stage — on top of inference. An edge deployment pays that on the camera box.
pros: full video retained centrally for forensics
cons: needs ~0.80 Gbps of sustained, reliable city-wide uplink
a network outage blinds the whole system
central decode compute is pure overhead

edge_architecture.description: Inference runs on the camera or a nearby edge box; only structured VehicleEvent JSON is sent centrally.

edge_nodes.unit: edge inference nodes of the measured class
edge_nodes.formula: same worker count as the central case — the compute does not disappear, it relocates
edge_nodes.caveat: If each camera gets its own box, the count is the camera count and each box is mostly idle; consolidating several cameras per box is what makes the worker count the right number.

pros: uplink drops by the ratio below — ordinary 4G/broadband suffices
video need never leave the pole (privacy + retention cost)
cons: model updates must be pushed to N nodes
per-node hardware cost and physical maintenance
no central video for after-the-fact re-analysis

bandwidth_reduction_factor.unit: x less uplink for edge vs central

network_and_architecture.recommendation: Edge inference for scale, central for depth. The bandwidth ratio is large enough that a 2000-camera city is a networking problem in the central design and a fleet-management problem in the edge design — the latter is the cheaper problem. A hybrid (edge inference plus on-demand video pull for flagged events only) keeps the forensic capability without the sustained uplink.
network_and_architecture.cost_note: Deliberately no currency figures: we did not measure or quote hardware or bandwidth prices, and inventing them would undermine every measured number above. The figures here are quantities — GPUs, cores, GB, Gbps — which a procurement price list turns into money.

ingest_headroom_ratio.caveat: Above 1.0 means one backend process on this laptop already keeps up. Below 1.0 means the write path needs sharding or Postgres + batching.

bytes_per_event.method: derived from an actual sqlite database file size / row count

storage.caveat: Structured events only. Storing plate crops or video clips is orders of magnitude larger and is a separate decision — a 50 KB JPEG per event would multiply this by ~100x.

measured_pipeline_ms.method: decode p50 0.9 + inference 48.0 + ingest p95 2.29 — measured stages, summed

max_queue_depth_frames.unit: frames of backlog a worker may hold
max_queue_depth_frames.caveat: Exceeding this means the plate arrives after the operator needs it, even though throughput looks fine. This is why sizing uses p95 and 70% headroom.

latency.note: This is the single-pass processing cost, not wall-clock photon-to-dashboard: it excludes camera encoder delay and network transit, which we cannot measure without real cameras.

central_architecture.description: Every camera streams video to a central GPU cluster, which decodes and runs ANPR.
central_architecture.extra_central_cost: The cluster also pays video DECODE for every analysed frame — measured separately in the anpr suite's decode stage — on top of inference. An edge deployment pays that on the camera box.
pros: full video retained centrally for forensics
cons: needs ~8.00 Gbps of sustained, reliable city-wide uplink
a network outage blinds the whole system
central decode compute is pure overhead

edge_architecture.description: Inference runs on the camera or a nearby edge box; only structured VehicleEvent JSON is sent centrally.

edge_nodes.unit: edge inference nodes of the measured class
edge_nodes.formula: same worker count as the central case — the compute does not disappear, it relocates
edge_nodes.caveat: If each camera gets its own box, the count is the camera count and each box is mostly idle; consolidating several cameras per box is what makes the worker count the right number.

pros: uplink drops by the ratio below — ordinary 4G/broadband suffices
video need never leave the pole (privacy + retention cost)
cons: model updates must be pushed to N nodes
per-node hardware cost and physical maintenance
no central video for after-the-fact re-analysis

bandwidth_reduction_factor.unit: x less uplink for edge vs central

network_and_architecture.recommendation: Edge inference for scale, central for depth. The bandwidth ratio is large enough that a 2000-camera city is a networking problem in the central design and a fleet-management problem in the edge design — the latter is the cheaper problem. A hybrid (edge inference plus on-demand video pull for flagged events only) keeps the forensic capability without the sustained uplink.
network_and_architecture.cost_note: Deliberately no currency figures: we did not measure or quote hardware or bandwidth prices, and inventing them would undermine every measured number above. The figures here are quantities — GPUs, cores, GB, Gbps — which a procurement price list turns into money.
